title: Bangladesh approves Chinese state firm's LNG terminal at a fee 35% above existing ones
dek: A cabinet committee cleared CNEE's floating terminal at Maheshkhali without a tender or a price cut. It would be China's first LNG import terminal in Bangladesh, on the Bay of Bengal coast.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Bangladesh's government has approved a proposal from a Chinese state-owned company to build and run a floating liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal off Maheshkhali island in Cox's Bazar, at a daily fee 35-37% higher than the country pays for its two existing terminals, according to reports of the decision.

The Cabinet Committee on Government Purchase, chaired by Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury, cleared the project on Thursday, the finance ministry said, according to reports. The committee had sent the same proposal back on 14 October for a review of its financial terms. It was approved this time without a cut in cost.

## The deal

The company is China National Energy Engineering and Construction Co Ltd (CNEE). It proposed a floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) at Kutubjom off Maheshkhali on a build-own-operate basis, with a base capacity of 600 million cubic feet of gas a day and a peak of 750, and operations expected in 2028, according to reports.

Reports put the cost to Bangladesh at Tk 12,324 crore (about $988 million) over a 15-year contract, or Tk 13,161 crore over 20 years. The 15-year option carries a fee of $342,000 a day. Bangladesh pays $254,000 a day to the US firm Excelerate Energy for its 600-million-cubic-feet terminal, and about $249,000 a day to Summit LNG for a 500-million-cubic-feet unit. A state feasibility study in 2025 put a benchmark of about $240,000 a day, according to one report, which also listed cheaper offers in government papers, including $190,000 from Aramco Trading Singapore and $225,000 from another Chinese state firm, CMC.

The proposal was handled as a government-to-government deal without competitive bidding, under the Public Procurement Act's provisions for direct procurement. One report said the government's own negotiating committee could not determine how much of the extra cost was justified.

## Why Dhaka wants it

Bangladesh is short of gas. Reports put demand at about 3,800 million cubic feet a day against supply of about 2,700. A fire at Excelerate's terminal on 21 July halved the country's capacity to bring in imported LNG for a time. The government plans three or four more floating terminals.

Critics say the decision ignores cheaper options. M Shamsul Alam, energy adviser to the Consumers Association of Bangladesh, said the outcome "appeared predetermined", according to one report. The US ambassador, Brent Christensen, had called in September for a "transparent, competitive" process for new terminals.

## What it means for India and Bengal

The terminal would give a Chinese state company a 15- to 20-year operating role in Bangladesh's energy supply chain at Maheshkhali, on the Bay of Bengal coast near the Matarbari deep-sea port that Japan is financing. It adds to Chinese state firms' growing footprint in Bangladesh's energy infrastructure, a sector where India also competes for influence through cross-border electricity sales and a diesel pipeline from Assam. A higher fee paid for imported gas also feeds into Bangladesh's power subsidy bill, which in turn affects the country's ability to pay for electricity it buys from Indian suppliers.

Neither CNEE nor China's embassy in Dhaka had commented publicly on the approval in the reports reviewed. Beijing has generally described its projects in Bangladesh as commercial cooperation that helps the country's development.

## What happens next

The approval clears the way for contract signing. The government has not announced a signing date or a final contract term.
